assessor: AI implementation assistant (Codex), qualitative review of saved titles and supplied abstracts
limitations: Assistant-authored, unblinded judgments on a constructed set used during development. Identical abstracts for ON06/ON09 were checked and prior rationales reused. No independent clinical adjudication, full-text appraisal, exhaustive relevant set, recall estimate, or controlled improvement claim. No new answer-quality score is assigned. The source-attribution diagnostic is reported separately and remains a known failure.

assessments.coverage_rationale: The narrative review supports recognized nutritional assessment and multidisciplinary classification, but the set lacks a clear routine screening/repeat-assessment pathway or a direct demonstration that normal BMI excludes nothing. Prognostic and postoperative material is partial; two prevention/obesity records do not fit the case.
assessments.search_findings: A broader Boolean query returned five records, but CRC prevention, obesity and postoperative treatment topics reduced precision.

paper_assessments.rationale: The narrative review addresses malnutrition/cachexia/sarcopenia classification, risk, intake and cancer/treatment-related influences, with multidisciplinary assessment. These are central to the nutrition assessment question; the abstract does not specify the complete screening workflow or a normal-BMI rule.

The CRC cachexia cohort connects inflammation and performance status to prognosis. It provides functional/inflammatory context but is not a study of routine nutrition screening or a diagnostic rule for this early-treatment patient.

The review concerns nutritional prevention of colorectal cancer, chemoprevention and cancer-risk reduction. It does not address malnutrition screening for an adult already losing weight during treatment.

The postoperative CRC nutrition trial uses a nutritional-risk tool and reports muscle/chemotherapy outcomes, so it relates to assessment and follow-up. Its main question is an ONS intervention after surgery, not the initial chemotherapy screening decision or normal-BMI interpretation.

This obesity/cancer-risk review addresses carcinogenesis and prevention rather than cancer-treatment malnutrition assessment. Intentional weight loss in healthy people or survivors should not be imported into the case.

assessments.coverage_rationale: The human studies inform variability and uncertainty of measured versus predicted resting expenditure. None establishes the requested daily protein/energy targets or calculation; two animal studies are not applicable.
assessments.search_findings: The tagged query remained focused on cachexia and calorimetry, returning three human metabolism papers and two preclinical records rather than an adult nutrition-target guideline.

paper_assessments.rationale: The human observational study relates measured versus predicted REE and metabolic abnormalities to treatment toxicity. It informs limitations and the need for individual assessment, but does not supply daily energy/protein targets.
The study concerns bone-metastasis cachexia, mitochondria and energy metabolism in mice. It cannot inform human daily energy/protein target calculation for a 60-kg adult.
The rat tumor/cachexia calorimetry experiment is preclinical and describes metabolic phases. It does not establish adult oncology nutrition requirements or protein targets.

The large human cancer/control study shows variability in resting energy expenditure and body composition. It is relevant to prediction limitations, but does not establish total daily energy requirements or protein intake targets.

The human cachexia study documents disagreement between predicted and measured resting energy expenditure. This supports caution about estimates, not the specific daily kcal/kg and protein calculation.

assessments.coverage_rationale: The set describes dysphagia, malnutrition, nutritional-support context and refeeding caution, but no supplied abstract directly establishes the requested EN-first escalation or when PN is appropriate with a functioning intestine. One letter has no abstract.
assessments.search_findings: The query combined head/neck, enteral and parenteral concepts, yet returned mainly older esophageal/surgical records and a refeeding case report. No second search was requested.

paper_assessments.rationale: The esophageal-cancer review describes dysphagia and nutrition-support methods. It is related background, but the tumor/treatment context differs and the supplied abstract does not specify EN-versus-PN escalation for head/neck radiotherapy.

Only an esophageal-cancer letter/comment title is available; there is no supplied abstract demonstrating a connection to nutrition route selection. The rating is based on metadata alone, not unseen full text.
The head/neck-cancer refeeding case report provides a relevant safety consideration when commencing EN or PN. It does not answer which route should follow failed oral nutrition in a functioning gut.

The old laryngopharyngeal/cervical-esophageal surgical series discusses malnutrition and nutritional preparation. Surgical reconstruction and postoperative radiotherapy differ from the present route-escalation decision, and the abstract lacks the requested EN/PN criteria.

The old postoperative esophageal-cancer PN study relates dysphagia, weight loss and nitrogen balance to support needs. This is peripheral nutrition-support context; its postoperative targets cannot be applied as current head/neck radiotherapy route guidance.

assessments.coverage_rationale: A directly relevant MBO review addresses prognosis and selected PN/palliative decisions, but its emphasis on surgical/curative candidates leaves nonsurgical intestinal-failure selection, individualized goals and burden/benefit uncertainties only partly represented.
assessments.search_findings: The broader advanced-cancer alternative brought in cachexia guidance, generic PN, a truncated conference collection and a swallowing-function study.

paper_assessments.rationale: The ASCO guideline concerns advanced-cancer cachexia and discourages routine artificial feeding for cachexia alone. That is a useful distinction, but the case concerns obstructive intestinal failure, so the abstract is not a blanket reason to deny PN here; its 2020 drug statement also predates later updates.

The MBO review explicitly discusses prognosis, PN candidate selection, obstruction management and palliative/hospice discussions. It directly fits the main decision, while its surgical/curative emphasis and abstract-only detail limit broad application to persistent nonsurgical obstruction.

The supplied truncated intensive-care proceedings excerpt lists sepsis/biomarker topics and offers no assessable malignant-obstruction PN decision evidence. No inference is made about unseen items elsewhere in the collection.

The general PN review mentions the role of nutrition teams and possible justification of long-term IV nutrition in cancer. It is background, not a prognosis/goals-based framework for malignant obstruction.
The study concerns chronic dysphagia and gastrostomy dependence after oropharyngeal chemoradiation, not malignant bowel obstruction, intestinal failure, prognosis or PN goals-of-care decisions.

assessments.coverage_rationale: The ESPEN position paper and two cancer-muscle/nutrition reviews address multimodal management, assessment, metabolic/inflammatory context and limited evidence. This substantially covers calorie-only limitations and supportive care, while specific current pharmacology and case-tailored choices are absent.
assessments.search_findings: The ungrouped OR treatment expanded the query to more than fourteen million matches. Two ranked records on scars and menopausal hormone therapy were off-topic; the other three were useful.

paper_assessments.rationale: The ESPEN expert paper explicitly supports early nutrition-risk screening, broader anorexia/body-composition/inflammation/function assessment and multimodal individualized intervention. It directly addresses the supportive approach beyond calories.

The review covers low muscle mass in cancer, nutrition requirements, multimodal interventions and weak/limited oncology-specific evidence. These are directly useful to the supportive-care and uncertainty components; listed supplements/doses are not thereby validated for this patient.
The review concerns hypertrophic scars and keloid treatment algorithms, not cancer cachexia or oncology nutrition. The broad OR branch is a plausible reason for this off-topic match.

The chemotherapy-sarcopenia review links muscle loss with nutrition, exercise and coordinated multidisciplinary care. It directly supports a multimodal approach but is not a validated intervention prescription for metastatic lung cancer.
The menopausal-hormone-therapy overview addresses vasomotor symptoms, osteoporosis and hormone risks/benefits. It does not address the cachexia nutrition/supportive-care decision.

assessments.coverage_rationale: The relevant refeeding reviews cover risk identification, cautious reintroduction, vitamins, individualized support and monitoring. The set also contains pediatric and surgical mismatches, and one truncated unrelated conference collection.
assessments.search_findings: The revised run retrieved the same papers and identical supplied abstracts as the initial run; order and query details are retained in this record. Five of eight matches were fetched. The ranking included a conference proceedings record whose huge abstract was truncated by the tool; it supplied no usable refeeding evidence in the shown excerpt.

paper_assessments.rationale: The preoperative-PN review mentions preventing refeeding complications with micronutrient management and monitoring. It is primarily about surgical PN efficacy and duration, not safe initiation for a severely undernourished adult; routine adequate-energy advice cannot be imported into this high-risk case.

The pediatric-oncology consensus discusses malnutrition assessment and nutrition interventions, including refeeding among its search topics. The pediatric population and abstract lacking a specific adult restart/monitoring regimen make it partial background.

The cancer-relevant refeeding review explicitly addresses rapid-feeding risk, cautious initiation, slow increase, thiamine and electrolyte/fluid management. It is directly useful to the core principles, although the 2009 abstract is not an individualized prescription or a substitute for current protocols.

This is a broad intensive-care conference proceedings collection. The supplied 4,500-character excerpt lists unrelated sepsis/biomarker abstracts and contains no assessable refeeding management evidence. This rating concerns the shown material, not a claim that no relevant item exists elsewhere in the enormous collection.

The hematological-cancer refeeding review emphasizes risk identification, individualized nutrition and ongoing monitoring. These central preventive principles fit the question, while the abstract provides limited operational dosing and electrolyte detail.

assessments.coverage_rationale: The ASCO guideline directly addresses routine neutropenic diets and infection, with historical infection-prevention context. The new query does not retrieve the conflicting 2026 trial seen in the initial run; current subgroup uncertainty and detailed safe-food implementation remain incomplete.
assessments.search_findings: Five papers were returned, including a global-risk analysis, an animal microbiome study and a truncated proceedings collection. More matches did not ensure clinically coherent selection.

paper_assessments.rationale: The adult active-treatment ASCO guideline explicitly reports and recommends against routine neutropenic diets for infection prevention. It directly addresses the restriction question, but its search cutoff predates the newer conflicting high-risk-population trial observed in the first run.

The GBD analysis evaluates global population risk factors and disease burden. Its truncated abstract does not concern chemotherapy neutropenia or a clinical comparison of fresh-produce restriction with food-safety precautions.

The older bacteremia review relates granulocytopenia, colonization and historical hand/food/water prevention practices. It provides context, but no modern randomized comparison or practical evidence-based produce guidance.

This antibiotic/diet microbiome-recovery experiment is in mice and compares dietary environments with microbial transplantation. It does not address adult chemotherapy neutropenia or neutropenic-diet efficacy.
The supplied truncated congress collection covers many unrelated health topics and contains no assessable neutropenic-diet evidence. Unseen content is not assumed to support the case.

assessments.coverage_rationale: One breast-cancer supplement-safety review addresses antioxidant/treatment interference, with indirect pediatric uncertainty context. No returned abstract directly establishes the food-versus-high-dose vitamin distinction or regimen-specific interaction evidence.
assessments.search_findings: The query now returned some oncology-supplement material but also reproductive-herbal and probiotic-mechanistic records; five returned papers should not be mistaken for five applicable clinical sources.

paper_assessments.rationale: The berberine review concerns a pharmacologically active nutrition supplement, antioxidant/anti-inflammatory mechanisms and possible cancer applications. It is related background, not evidence about high-dose antioxidant vitamins during chemotherapy.

The breast-cancer supplement-safety review explicitly discusses antioxidants potentially interfering with ROS-dependent cancer therapy, conflicting safety evidence and oncologist oversight. It directly informs the interaction/caution discussion, although its hair-loss context and broad supplement categories limit generalization.
The Cistanches herbal review focuses on infertility/reproductive outcomes. Antioxidant mechanisms and cancer mentions do not supply evidence for the requested chemotherapy-vitamin safety question.

The pediatric-cancer CAM review discusses inadequate supplement safety/efficacy and chemotherapy-interaction evidence. These uncertainties are relevant background, but the pediatric population and broad older supplement scope limit application to an adult high-dose-vitamin question.
The probiotic cancer review concerns microbial interventions and mechanistic effects. It does not answer antioxidant-vitamin dosing, equivalence to food, or chemotherapy interaction safety.

assessments.coverage_rationale: The PEI guideline and reviews directly cover maldigestion/steatorrhea, weight loss, assessment, PERT and dietary support. A pediatric pancreatitis review is indirect; abstracts do not establish a patient-specific dose or oncology-specific follow-up plan.
assessments.search_findings: The revised run retrieved the same papers and identical supplied abstracts as the initial run; order and query details are retained in this record. Five PMIDs were ranked; one was excluded because no parseable journal-article record was returned. Four papers remained, including one pediatric mismatch.

paper_assessments.rationale: The multidisciplinary PEI guideline explicitly links symptoms/nutritional assessment to diagnosis and identifies PERT plus dietary support as core treatment. It directly informs the potentially treatable maldigestion problem, though the abstract lacks condition-specific dosing and follow-up.

The review links pancreatic dysfunction, steatorrhea, malnutrition and enzyme therapy, but concerns children with recurrent/chronic pancreatitis rather than adults with unresectable pancreatic cancer. It is indirect background.

The exocrine-dysfunction staging review describes steatorrhea, weight loss, nutritional deficiencies and PERT. These are central to the case; proposed staging details and differential testing are not equivalent to a cancer-specific validated management protocol.

The review explicitly identifies pancreatic cancer among PEI causes, the case symptoms and enzyme therapy as central treatment. It is directly relevant, without supplying an individualized regimen or proving efficacy for this exact patient.

assessments.coverage_rationale: One cancer-specific ketogenic-diet review addresses proposed mechanisms, cachexia/obesity contexts and complications. The set lacks applicable fasting-around-chemotherapy trials or clear evidence in already weight-losing adults; four weight-management/PCOS records are off-topic.
assessments.search_findings: Grouping fasting and ketogenic diet with OR avoided the empty initial result, but the broad query returned several obesity-drug and PCOS papers. No additional refinement was requested.

paper_assessments.rationale: The STEP 8 trial compares semaglutide and liraglutide for intentional weight loss in adults with obesity. It does not evaluate fasting/KD around chemotherapy or cancer outcomes in an adult already losing weight.

The review explicitly covers ketogenic diets in cancer, proposed antitumor mechanisms, cachexia/obesity contexts and complications. It directly informs the evidence/uncertainty discussion, but its abstract does not demonstrate routine clinical benefit or safety for this case.

The time-restricted-eating review concerns obesity, diabetes and PCOS weight management. It contains no supplied oncology or chemotherapy evidence and cannot justify restriction in this malnutrition-risk case.
The semaglutide appetite/energy-intake trial is in people with obesity and evaluates a weight-loss drug, not fasting or ketogenic diets during cancer treatment.

The dietary-intervention review concerns PCOS, insulin resistance and intentional weight management. It does not inform cancer treatment outcomes or the safety of restriction for this already weight-losing adult.
